intro: Nine problems in the style of the Finnish matriculation examination bring together the lesson's energy, power and efficiency. Solve them as in the exam: justify the choice of model, solve for the quantity asked before substituting the numbers and assess whether the result is reasonable. The seventh problem is an applied source-based task whose source opens from the link in the task. In the last two problems you read the data from a figure. Open the model answer and the scoring guide only when your solution is ready.

tasks.title: Solar power at the cottage
tasks.source_note: The cottage, the devices and the production figures are invented examples that match the order of magnitude of an ordinary small solar power system.
tasks.text:
A summer cottage on an island has no connection to the power grid. On the roof are solar panels with a rated power of $1.2\,\text{kW}$. The electricity from the panels is stored in a battery, and an inverter converts the battery's electricity into a form suitable for the devices. The combined efficiency of charging and discharging the battery is $90\,\%$ and that of the inverter $93\,\%$.

The cottage's electrical devices on an ordinary summer day:

| Device | Power | Use per day |
|---|---|---|
| fridge | $45\,\text{W}$ | $24\,\text{h}$ |
| LED lamps | $6 \cdot 7.0\,\text{W}$ | $5.0\,\text{h}$ |
| coffee maker | $1.0\,\text{kW}$ | $15\,\text{min}$ |

The power of the fridge is an average power, because its compressor runs only part of the time.

The panels' display shows that on a sunny day the panels produced $5.4\,\text{kWh}$ and on a cloudy day $1.5\,\text{kWh}$.

parts.text: How much electrical energy do the cottage's devices use in a day?
hints: Each device has a power and a running time. Which quantity tells you how much energy a device uses in that time, and what do you do with the devices' energies at the end?
The electrical energy of a device is power times time: $E = P\,t$. Find the energy of each device separately and add the energies together.
The coffee maker runs for only $15\,\text{min}$ and its power is in kilowatts: convert the time to hours before multiplying. There are six lamps, so their combined power is $6 \cdot 7.0\,\text{W}$.

criteria.detail: The energy of each device is $E = P\,t$, and the energies are added up.
Fridge $1.08\,\text{kWh}$, lamps $0.21\,\text{kWh}$ and coffee maker $0.25\,\text{kWh}$; minutes converted to hours.
$1.5\,\text{kWh}$ (about $5.5\,\text{MJ}$) to two significant figures.

parts.text: How much electricity must the panels produce in a day so that the need in part a is covered through the battery and the inverter? Is the production of a cloudy day enough?
hints: The energy flows from the panels through the battery and the inverter to the devices. Must the panels produce more or less energy than the devices use?
The stages are in series, so the efficiencies are multiplied: $E_\text{panels} = \dfrac{E_\text{need}}{\eta_\text{batt}\,\eta_\text{inv}}$.

First calculate the combined efficiency $\eta_\text{batt}\,\eta_\text{inv}$, then the energy of the panels. Compare the result with the production of the cloudy day: how much of the cloudy day's energy reaches the devices?

criteria.text: Justifies that the battery and the inverter are in series, so their efficiencies are multiplied.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{panels} = \dfrac{E_\text{need}}{\eta_\text{batt}\,\eta_\text{inv}}$
$E_\text{panels} \approx 1.8\,\text{kWh}$
The $1.5\,\text{kWh}$ of a cloudy day is not enough: only about $1.3\,\text{kWh}$ of it reaches the devices, so the battery runs down unless the surplus of a sunny day is in storage.

parts.text: The cottage's neighbour says: “The panels' power is $1.2\,\text{kW}$, so they produce $1.2\,\text{kWh}$ a day.” Evaluate the claim.
hints: The neighbour treats the kilowatt and the kilowatt-hour as if they were the same thing. Which one tells how fast energy is produced, and which one tells the amount of energy?
Energy is power times time: $E = P\,t$. The rated power is the greatest power the panels can produce.

Calculate how many hours at rated power would correspond to the $5.4\,\text{kWh}$ of the sunny day and to the $1.5\,\text{kWh}$ of the cloudy day. What do the numbers tell you about the neighbour's claim?

criteria.text: Tells power and energy apart: the kilowatt tells the rate of production, the kilowatt-hour the amount of energy; energy is power multiplied by time.
Uses the data: on a sunny day $5.4\,\text{kWh}$ corresponds to $4.5$ hours at rated power, on a cloudy day only about one hour.

criteria.detail: The claim is wrong: the day's energy depends on how strongly and how long the sun shines, and the rated power is the maximum power.

tasks.title: The wood chip power plant
tasks.source_note: The plant and its numbers are invented examples. The heat of combustion of forest chips, $9.5\,\text{MJ/kg}$, is typical of moist chips, and the actual value varies with the moisture content.
tasks.text:
A town's combined heat and power plant burns forest chips and produces both electricity and district heat. On a frosty day the following were read from the screen in the plant's control room:

- chips are fed into the boiler at $42\,\text{t}$ per hour
- heat of combustion of the chips $9.5\,\text{MJ/kg}$
- electrical power $30\,\text{MW}$
- district heating power $70\,\text{MW}$

For comparison, the same electricity could be produced in a condensing power plant with an efficiency of $38\,\%$, and the same district heat in a boiler producing only heat, with an efficiency of $90\,\%$.

parts.text: How large is the fuel power of the plant?
hints: Wood chips contain chemical energy, and they are fed into the boiler all the time. Which quantity tells how much energy arrives every second, and what do you need to calculate it?
The energy of the burned chips is the heating value times the mass: $Q = Hm$. Power is energy divided by time: $P_0 = \dfrac{Q}{t}$.
Convert the mass burned in an hour from tonnes to kilograms and the hour to seconds, $t = 3600\,\text{s}$. Then calculate the energy of one hour and divide it by the time.

criteria.detail: $Q = Hm$ for the chips burnt in an hour and $P_0 = \dfrac{Q}{t}$
$P_0 \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^{2}\,\text{MW}$ (more precisely $110.8\,\text{MW}$)

parts.text: Calculate the electrical efficiency and the overall efficiency of the plant.
hints: Efficiency tells what fraction of the fuel power is put to use. What counts as useful in the electrical efficiency, and what in the total efficiency?

$\eta = \dfrac{P_\text{useful}}{P_0}$: for the electrical efficiency the useful part is the electric power $P_\text{el}$, and for the total efficiency the electric and district-heating power together, $\eta_\text{tot} = \dfrac{P_\text{el} + P_\text{dh}}{P_0}$.
Use the fuel power of part a as the denominator. Calculate the total useful power $P_\text{el} + P_\text{dh}$ first and divide only then.

criteria.detail: $\eta_\text{el} = \dfrac{P_\text{el}}{P_0}$ and $\eta_\text{tot} = \dfrac{P_\text{el} + P_\text{dh}}{P_0}$
Both efficiencies from the fuel power of part a.
$\eta_\text{el} \approx 27\,\%$ and $\eta_\text{tot} \approx 90\,\%$

parts.text: How many tonnes of chips per hour would be needed if the same electricity and the same district heat were produced separately in a condensing power plant and a heating boiler?
hints: In separate production each plant needs its own fuel. How do you find the fuel power when the useful power and the efficiency are known?
The fuel power of each plant is $P_0 = \dfrac{P_\text{useful}}{\eta}$, and the powers are added together. The mass of chips is $m = \dfrac{P_0\,t}{H}$.

First calculate the fuel power of the condensing plant and of the heat boiler separately, and their sum. Then calculate the energy of one hour and the mass of chips, and convert it to tonnes. Compare the result with the $42\,\text{t}$ of the combined production.

criteria.text: Solves the fuel power of each plant separately from its useful power, $P_0 = P_\text{a} : \eta$, and adds them up.

criteria.detail: about $59\,\text{t}$ per hour, that is, about $17\,\text{t}$ more than in combined heat and power

parts.text: In summer district heat is needed only for hot tap water. Explain why the overall efficiency of the plant does not then stay the same if it produces the same electrical power.
hints: Where does the heat of the condenser go in summer, when there is no need for district heating? Who makes use of it then?
Only the power that ends up as useful is counted in the total efficiency: $\eta_\text{tot} = \dfrac{P_\text{el} + P_\text{dh}}{P_0}$. What happens to the numerator when $P_\text{dh}$ gets smaller?
Write the expression of the total efficiency for the case $P_\text{dh}$ small or zero and compare it with the efficiencies of part b. What should be considered in running the plant then?

criteria.text: Explains that the heat of the condenser is useful only when there is a use for it as district heat; otherwise it must be given off to the surroundings as waste heat.

criteria.detail: The overall efficiency falls towards the electrical efficiency, so in summer the plant is run at a lower power or the electricity is produced elsewhere.

tasks.title: Frost and the electricity bill
tasks.source_note: The data are an invented example: the numbers are calculated from a model in which the other electricity consumption is about $12\,\text{kWh}$ a day and the heating increases steadily as the outdoor temperature falls, and variation like that of measurements has been added to them.
tasks.text:
A detached house is heated with direct electric heating, and the indoor temperature is kept at $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The electricity company's app shows the house's electricity consumption day by day. For one week in January the family recorded the daily consumption $E$ and the average outdoor temperature $T$ of the day. The electricity consumption other than heating, such as lighting, cooking and appliances, is about $12\,\text{kWh}$ a day in the house.

| Day | $T\ ({}^\circ\text{C})$ | $E\ (\text{kWh})$ |
|---|---|---|
| 7 Jan | $-4$ | $112$ |
| 8 Jan | $-10$ | $139$ |
| 9 Jan | $-16$ | $174$ |
| 10 Jan | $-19$ | $186$ |
| 11 Jan | $-13$ | $155$ |
| 12 Jan | $-7$ | $126$ |
| 13 Jan | $-1$ | $100$ |
| 14 Jan | $2$ | $83$ |

parts.text: Present the daily consumption as a function of the outdoor temperature in a graph, and fit a suitable model to the points.
hints: Which quantity is independent and which is dependent? What happens to the consumption when the temperature changes?
Plot the points in a $(T,\,E)$ coordinate system and fit a line $E = kT + b$ to them. The line passes between the points, and the points are not joined into a broken line.
The horizontal axis must reach negative temperatures. Label the axes with the quantity and its unit and choose scales so that the points fill the graph.

criteria.detail: On the horizontal axis $T\ ({}^\circ\text{C})$ with its negative values, on the vertical axis $E\ (\text{kWh})$.
A falling straight line is fitted to the points, passing between them; the points are not joined into a broken line.

parts.text: Determine the slope of the line from the graph. By how much does the heating power increase for each kelvin the outdoor temperature falls? Answer in watts per kelvin.
hints: What does the slope of the line tell about the change of energy as the temperature changes? From which points of the graph should you read the slope?
The slope is $k = \dfrac{\Delta E}{\Delta T}$. Read it from two points of the line that are far apart. Average power is energy divided by time: $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$.

The unit of the slope is the energy of a day per degree, $\text{kWh}/{}^\circ\text{C}$. Divide it by the length of a day, $24\,\text{h}$, and convert to watts. A change of one degree Celsius equals a change of one kelvin.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(-20\,{}^\circ\text{C};\ 191\,\text{kWh})$ and $(0\,{}^\circ\text{C};\ 93\,\text{kWh})$: about $-4.9\,\text{kWh}/{}^\circ\text{C}$ per day.

criteria.text: Interprets the slope: the daily heating energy increases by about $4.9\,\text{kWh}$ when the outdoor temperature falls by one kelvin.

criteria.detail: The average power is the energy divided by the time: $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$, $t = 24\,\text{h}$.
$4.9\,\text{kWh} : 24\,\text{h} \approx 0.20\,\text{kW}$, that is, about $200\,\text{W}$ per kelvin; a result of $192$–$216\,\text{W/K}$ is accepted.

parts.text: Use the graph to estimate the house's electricity consumption on a day whose average temperature is $-28\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Assess how reliable the estimate is.
hints: The measurements cover only a certain temperature range. What does it mean to extend the line beyond the measured range, and how certain is that?
Use the equation of the line $E = kT + b$ or extend the line on the graph. The slope $k$ is the result of part b, and $b$ is the value of the line at $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
Substitute $T = -28\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Find how many kelvins this is below the coldest measured point, and consider whether the line is likely to stay straight in such cold.

criteria.detail: The line has been extended outside the measured range, or the equation of the line $E = kT + b$ has been used.

The estimate is an extrapolation $9\,\text{K}$ outside the measured range, so it holds only if the model stays a straight line; a strong wind or the maximum power of the heaters can change the result.

parts.text: At what outdoor temperature would the house, according to the model, need no heating at all? Explain why this temperature is not the same as the indoor temperature $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
hints: When does the house need no heating at all? How much electricity use is then left?

When no heating is needed, only the other electricity use, which the task gives, is left. Solve from the equation of the line $E = kT + b$, or read from the graph, the temperature at which $E$ has this value.
Compare the temperature you found with the indoor temperature $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. What other than the heating brings energy into the house, and what does conservation of energy say about it?

criteria.detail: The temperature at which $E = 12\,\text{kWh}$ is read from the line: about $16$–$17\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

criteria.text: Explains with conservation of energy: the electrical energy of the appliances, the heat of the people and solar radiation increase the internal energy of the house, so they make up for part of the heat losses.

criteria.detail: Heating is needed only when the outdoor temperature is below about $17\,{}^\circ\text{C}$; the accuracy of the model is limited by, for example, the sun and the wind, which the data do not separate.

tasks.title: The island's electricity
tasks.source_note: The island, the options and their numbers are invented examples. The emission factor of diesel is a rounded order-of-magnitude value.
tasks.text:
An island in an archipelago municipality has $400$ inhabitants. Its electricity is now produced in a diesel power plant. The island's electricity consumption is $3.0\,\text{GWh}$ a year, and the winter consumption peak is $1.2\,\text{MW}$. The municipality is comparing three options.

| Option | Power |
|---|---|
| A: diesel power plant (current) | $1.5\,\text{MW}$ |
| B: wind turbines and a battery | $2 \cdot 1.0\,\text{MW}$ |
| C: submarine cable to the mainland | $5\,\text{MW}$ |

- A: emission factor about $700\,\text{g/kWh}$, the fuel is brought by ship.
- B: the average power of the wind turbines is about $30\,\%$ of the rated power, and the battery holds $2.0\,\text{MWh}$.
- C: the cable is $12\,\text{km}$ long and the transmission loss is about $3\,\%$.

At the meeting of the municipal council two claims were made: “The wind turbines produce more in a year than the island consumes, so the diesel plant can be dismantled” and “Wind power is completely emission-free”.

parts.text: Evaluate the first claim. Justify your answer with a calculation.
hints: The claim contains two separate things: the wind produces enough energy in a year, and that is enough to remove the diesel. Is the energy of a year enough for the consumption? And is it enough at every moment?

Energy is average power times time: $E = P_\text{avg}\,t$. The average power of the wind turbines is $30\,\%$ of the rated power, and a year has $8760\,\text{h}$. The time the battery lasts at peak power is $t = \dfrac{E_\text{battery}}{P_\text{peak}}$.

First calculate the combined average power of the two turbines and then the energy of a year in gigawatt-hours; compare it with the consumption of $3.0\,\text{GWh}$. Then calculate for how many hours a full battery covers the peak of $1.2\,\text{MW}$.

criteria.text: Tells energy and power apart: production must match consumption at every moment, and in calm weather the wind turbines produce nothing.
Calculates that a full battery covers the $1.2\,\text{MW}$ peak for only $2.0\,\text{MWh} : 1.2\,\text{MW} \approx 1.7\,\text{h}$.

criteria.detail: The claim does not hold: the year's energy is enough, but for calm periods dispatchable power or a connection to the grid is needed.

parts.text: Compare the options using at least three criteria and make a reasoned recommendation.
hints: What must the energy system on the island be able to do at every moment? Where do A, B and C differ from each other?
Choose at least three criteria, for example controllability, security of supply, emissions, fuel transport or cost, and go through each option using the numbers of the data.

Make a small table of the comparison: the rows are the criteria and the columns the options. Justify each cell with a number from the data. The recommendation comes only after the table and follows from it.

criteria.text: Uses at least three criteria of comparison, for example controllability, security of supply, emissions, transport of fuel and price.
Justifies each comparison with the properties of the options, for example the cable brings the dispatchable power of the mainland grid and its loss is small.

criteria.detail: The recommendation follows from the comparison, for example the cable and wind power together and diesel as backup power.

parts.text: Evaluate the second claim. How large are the annual carbon dioxide emissions of the diesel power plant, and how are they compared with the emissions of wind power?
hints: Emissions depend on the energy produced and the emission factor. Does a wind turbine cause emissions only in use, or also before that?
The mass of the emissions is the emission factor times the energy: $m = e\,E$, where $e = 700\,\text{g/kWh}$ and $E$ is the island's yearly consumption.

Convert the energy from gigawatt-hours to kilowatt-hours, $1\,\text{GWh} = 10^{6}\,\text{kWh}$, before multiplying, and convert the grams to tonnes at the end. For the comparison, think what emissions arise from making and building a wind turbine.

criteria.text: Explains life-cycle emissions: manufacturing, transporting and building a wind turbine cause emissions even though operating it does not, so the emissions are not zero but are much smaller than those of diesel.

criteria.detail: The claim is inaccurate: wind power is low-emission, not emission-free.

tasks.title: The efficiency of a kettle
tasks.source_note: The report and its measurement results are invented examples.
tasks.text:
A group of students wanted to check the manufacturer's claim that an electric kettle “transfers more than $90\,\%$ of the electrical energy into the water”. An extract from the group's report:

> We filled the kettle's jug to $1.0$ litre by its scale with tap water at a temperature of $15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. We started the kettle and the timing at the same time. The kettle switched itself off when the water boiled, $3\,\text{min}\ 5\,\text{s}$ after starting. After the kettle had switched off, we opened the lid and measured the temperature of the water with a thermometer as $96\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The power on the kettle's rating plate is $2200\,\text{W}$. We calculated the efficiency as $83\,\%$, so the manufacturer's claim does not hold.

The specific heat capacity of water is $4190\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, and a litre of water weighs about $1.0\,\text{kg}$.

parts.text: Show how the group got $83\,\%$ as the efficiency.
hints: Efficiency compares the useful energy with the energy used. Which energy is the useful one here, and which one is the energy used?
$\eta = \dfrac{Q}{E}$, where the energy needed to heat the water is $Q = cm\Delta T$ and the electrical energy taken by the kettle is $E = P\,t$.
Calculate the change in temperature $\Delta T$ and convert the time to seconds ($3\,\text{min}\ 5\,\text{s}$). Then calculate $Q$ and $E$ separately before dividing.

criteria.detail: $\eta = \dfrac{Q}{E}$, where $Q = cm\Delta T$ and $E = P\,t$
$\eta \approx 0.83 = 83\,\%$ to two significant figures

parts.text: Assess whether the group's conclusion is justified. Name the most important sources of error in the measurement and tell in which direction each changes the result.
hints: Which number was actually measured, and which one was only read from the rating plate? Where does the measurement differ from what the calculation assumes?
Ask two things of each source of error: does it change the numerator $Q$ or the denominator $E$, and does it make the efficiency $\eta = \dfrac{Q}{E}$ larger or smaller?

Try one source of error at a time: substitute a slightly different value into the calculation and see by how many percentage points $\eta$ changes. What does this tell about whether one measurement can show the manufacturer's claim to be wrong?

criteria.detail: Names sources of error and tells in which direction each changes the result: for example, the temperature of the water was measured only after the kettle switched off, when the water had already cooled (makes the result smaller); the power on the rating plate is not a measured power (can change the result in either direction, because the actual power depends on the mains voltage); the amount of water was read from the jug's scale (either direction); part of the energy heated the jug (a real loss).

Assesses the size of the effect: for example, a power of $2100\,\text{W}$ would give $87\,\%$ and $1.05\,\text{kg}$ of water would give $88\,\%$, so the uncertainty of the result is several percentage points.
One measurement with such a large uncertainty is not enough to show that the claim is wrong.

parts.text: The group suspects that the efficiency depends on the amount of water. Plan an experiment that can find this out reliably.
hints: Which quantity changes when the amount of water varies, and what must stay the same so that the comparison is fair?

The quantity you change is the amount of water $m$ and the quantity you study is the efficiency $\eta = \dfrac{c\,m\,\Delta T}{E}$. Decide which quantities are measured and with what instrument, and which are kept constant.

Think when the temperature is read so that the reading is reliable, and how the electrical energy is measured. How many amounts of water do you need, what do you repeat and how do you present the results?

criteria.text: Varies only the amount of water (for example $0.50$–$1.5\,\text{kg}$) and keeps the other factors constant: the same initial temperature, the same kettle, the lid closed.

Measures the necessary quantities reliably: the mass with a balance, the electrical energy with an energy meter, the temperature of stirred water before boiling, for example when the water is at $80\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
Repeats the measurements and presents the results in a graph, for example the efficiency as a function of the amount of water, and assesses their uncertainty.

tasks.title: The pumped-storage plant in the mine
tasks.source_note: The mine and the plant's numbers are invented examples. The efficiencies are typical values for a pumped-storage plant.
tasks.text:
A pumped-storage power plant is being planned for a closed mine. The upper reservoir is at ground level, and the mine's tunnels $1.20\,\text{km}$ deeper serve as the lower reservoir. When electricity is needed, water from the upper reservoir flows down a pipe and turns a turbine and a generator at the bottom of the mine. When electricity is available cheaply, for example on a windy night, the same machines pump the water back up.

- volume of the upper reservoir $7.50 \cdot 10^{4}\,\text{m}^3$, density of water $1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$
- efficiency of the turbine and the generator $88\,\%$
- efficiency of the pump and the motor $85\,\%$
- the full upper reservoir is emptied steadily in $6.0$ hours

parts.text: How much potential energy does the water of the full upper reservoir have compared with the lower reservoir? Give the answer in megawatt-hours.
hints: Relative to what level does the water have potential energy? What do you need to know about the mass of the water?
$E_\text{p} = mgh$, where the mass is found from the density and the volume: $m = \rho V$.
Calculate the mass and convert the height to metres. The result is in joules; convert it to megawatt-hours: $1\,\text{MWh} = 10^{6}\,\text{W} \cdot 3600\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{p} = mgh$, where $m = \rho V$
$m = 7.50 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{kg}$ and $E_\text{p} \approx 8.83 \cdot 10^{11}\,\text{J}$

criteria.text: Converts the joules to megawatt-hours by substituting $1\,\text{MWh} = 10^{6}\,\text{W} \cdot 3600\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{p} \approx 245\,\text{MWh}$ to three significant figures

parts.text: How large is the electrical power of the plant when the reservoir is emptied?
hints: Not all of the potential energy comes out as electricity. Which factor tells what fraction becomes electricity, and over what time is the energy released?
The electrical energy is $\eta_\text{t}\,E_\text{p}$ and power is energy divided by time: $P = \dfrac{\eta_\text{t}\,E_\text{p}}{t}$.
Use the potential energy of part a and the turbine efficiency $0.88$ and divide by the time $6.0\,\text{h}$. If you keep the energy in megawatt-hours, you get the power directly in megawatts.

criteria.detail: $P = \dfrac{\eta_\text{t}\,E_\text{p}}{t}$
Electrical energy $0.88 \cdot 245\,\text{MWh} \approx 216\,\text{MWh}$
$P \approx 36\,\text{MW}$ to two significant figures like the time $6.0\,\text{h}$
For example, compared with the rated power of a wind turbine, the plant corresponds to about ten large wind turbines.

parts.text: How much electrical energy must be taken from the grid when the empty upper reservoir is pumped full? What is the overall efficiency of the storage when the reservoir is first filled and then emptied?
hints: In pumping, the energy flows the other way: from the grid to the motor and pump and on to the water. Must more or less energy be taken from the grid than ends up in the water?

In pumping, the useful energy is the potential energy of the water: $E_\text{grid} = \dfrac{E_\text{p}}{\eta_\text{p}}$. Filling and emptying the reservoir are stages in series, so the efficiencies are multiplied: $\eta = \eta_\text{p}\,\eta_\text{t}$.
First calculate $E_\text{grid}$ with the pump efficiency $0.85$. Check the overall efficiency by dividing the electrical energy obtained in emptying by the energy taken from the grid.

criteria.text: Justifies that pumping needs more electricity than the potential energy the water gains: $E_\text{grid} = E_\text{p} : \eta_\text{p}$.

criteria.detail: The overall efficiency is the product of the successive stages, $\eta = \eta_\text{p}\,\eta_\text{t}$.
$E_\text{grid} \approx 289\,\text{MWh}$
$\eta \approx 0.75 = 75\,\%$; check $216\,\text{MWh} : 289\,\text{MWh} \approx 0.75$

parts.text: The designer says: “The plant produces $216\,\text{MWh}$ of electricity every day.” Evaluate the claim and explain why the plant can still be useful.
hints: Can the plant produce energy? What does conservation of energy say about where the energy the plant gives out comes from?
Compare the energy taken from the grid when filling with the electrical energy obtained when emptying. What is their difference and where does it go?
Assess the benefit: when is electricity cheap or in surplus, when is it needed most, and how fast can the plant's power be adjusted? Reword the designer's claim so that it is correct.

criteria.text: States on the basis of conservation of energy that a pumped-storage plant does not produce energy but stores it: it takes more from the grid than it gives, about $73\,\text{MWh}$ in each filling and emptying.
Justifies the benefit: energy is shifted in time from moments of cheap overproduction to consumption peaks, and the plant is quickly controllable power alongside wind power.

criteria.detail: The claim is misleading; correctly: the plant gives $216\,\text{MWh}$ to the grid later from the $289\,\text{MWh}$ it took.

tasks.title: Why does the range of an electric car shrink in frost?
tasks.source_note: NAF and Motor, El Prix vinter 2026 (https://www.naf.no/elbil/elprix-nytt/elprix-vinter-2026). Checked 16 Nov 2026.
tasks.text:
On 28 January 2026 the Norwegian Automobile Federation NAF and the magazine Motor ran a winter test in which $24$ electric cars set off with a full battery from Oslo northwards into the mountains. Each car was driven until it could no longer move. Open [the results page of the test](https://www.naf.no/elbil/elprix-nytt/elprix-vinter-2026) and find the chart *Så langt kjørte bilene*. The page is in Norwegian, and you need these words: *rekkevidde* = range, *oppgitt* = stated, *målt* = measured, *avvik* = deviation. The stated range is the manufacturer's WLTP value, which is measured in a laboratory at room temperature.

According to the source (checked 16 Nov 2026):

- The temperature fell along the route: in Oslo it was about $-7\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and at the coldest point, Folldal, $-32\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
- The measured range of the cars was on average $38\,\%$ shorter than the stated one. In the winter test of 2025 the temperature was between $-6\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and $+8\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and the average deviation was $18\,\%$.
- The Hyundai Inster stopped at a point where the temperature was $-16\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The Lucid Air drove the furthest of the cars.
- The measured consumption was $21.2\,\text{kWh}$ for the Tesla Model Y and $21.6\,\text{kWh}$ for the Lucid Air per hundred kilometres.

| Car | Stated (WLTP) | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Hyundai Inster | $360\,\text{km}$ | $256\,\text{km}$ |
| Tesla Model Y | $629\,\text{km}$ | $359\,\text{km}$ |
| Lucid Air | $960\,\text{km}$ | $520\,\text{km}$ |

The internal resistance of a battery is larger when the battery is cold than when it is warm.

parts.text: Choose three electric cars from the chart of the source or use the cars of the table. Calculate by how many per cent the measured range of each car deviates from the stated one, and tell what the comparison shows.
hints: What do the stated and the measured range tell together? How is the difference expressed as a percentage when it is compared with the stated value?
The deviation as a percentage is $\dfrac{s_\text{meas} - s_\text{stated}}{s_\text{stated}} \cdot 100\,\%$. A negative result means that the measured distance is shorter than the stated one.

Put the stated and measured range of three cars of your choice into a table. For each, calculate the difference $s_\text{meas} - s_\text{stated}$ and divide it by the stated range. Finally, see whether the deviation varies from one car to another.

criteria.text: Picks the stated and the measured range of three cars from the source and presents them clearly, for example as a table.

criteria.detail: The difference is divided by the stated range: $\dfrac{s_\text{meas} - s_\text{stated}}{s_\text{stated}}$. For the cars of the table the results are about $-29\,\%$, $-43\,\%$ and $-46\,\%$; for other cars the numbers are different.
Every car drove a clearly shorter distance in the frost than stated, and the deviation varied from car to car from about $30\,\%$ to almost a half.

parts.text: The usable battery energy of an electric car is $75\,\text{kWh}$, and its range in mild weather is $450\,\text{km}$. Calculate the car's average energy consumption per hundred kilometres. Calculate also the consumption in frost, when the range is shorter by the test's average of $38\,\%$ and the battery is assumed to give the same energy. Assess how well the assumption holds.
hints: The energy of the battery and the range are proportional. How do you get the consumption per hundred kilometres when you know how far a full battery goes?

The consumption per hundred kilometres is $E_{100} = \dfrac{E\,s_{100}}{s}$, where $s_{100} = 100\,\text{km}$. In the cold the range is $s_\text{c} = (1 - 0.38)\,s$ and the energy of the battery is assumed to be the same.

First calculate the range in the cold $s_\text{c}$ and substitute it into the same formula. Then consider the assumption of the same battery energy: what happens to a cold battery, and in which direction would it change the calculated consumption?

criteria.detail: The energy is proportional to the distance: $E_{100} = \dfrac{E\,s_{100}}{s}$, and in frost the distance is $s_\text{c} = (1 - 0.38)\,s$.
$E_{100} \approx 16.7\,\text{kWh}$, $s_\text{c} = 279\,\text{km}$ and $E_{100,\text{c}} \approx 26.9\,\text{kWh}$
About $17\,\text{kWh}$ and $27\,\text{kWh}$ per hundred kilometres, two significant figures like the battery energy $75\,\text{kWh}$.
A cold battery gives less energy than a warm one, so part of the loss of range comes from the smaller energy and not from a larger consumption: the real consumption grows less than the model gives.

parts.text: Explain with thermal physics, electricity and mechanics why the energy consumption of an electric car per kilometre grows in frost.
hints: Think of three places where the cold increases energy consumption: the temperature difference between the car and the surroundings, the battery, and the motion. What is the phenomenon in each?

Thermal physics: the heat flow grows as the temperature difference grows. Electricity: power is $P = UI$ or the loss power $P = R_\text{s}I^2$. Mechanics: the work against resisting forces is $W = Fs$. Choose a suitable argument from each area.

Put the explanation together with conservation of energy: all the energy comes from the same battery. Write a chain in which some form of energy grows in each part, and conclude why less is left for driving.

criteria.text: Thermal physics: heat is transferred from the cabin and the battery to the surroundings the faster the larger the temperature difference is, so keeping the temperature takes heating power. In an electric car it is taken from the traction battery.

Electricity: gives at least one of these: the heater takes the power $P = UI$ from the battery for the whole drive, or the larger internal resistance of a cold battery increases the power $P = R_\text{s}I^2$, which becomes internal energy of the battery, and lowers the terminal voltage.

Mechanics: cold air is denser, so the air resistance is larger, and snow, slush and winter tyres increase the rolling resistance. At a steady speed the work $W = Fs$ against the resistive forces grows on every kilometre.

Brings the explanation together with the conservation of energy: all the energy is taken from the same battery, so the energy that goes to heating and to losses is not available for driving and the range shrinks.

parts.text: According to the test report, the range of the car that drove the furthest fell short of its stated range by $46\,\%$, which is one of the largest deviations in the test. Explain with the help of the source why this does not show that it withstands frost worse than the other cars.
hints: Study the information in the data: did all the cars drive in the same conditions along the whole route? At what temperature did each car drive?
Comparing the percentage deviations of the cars is fair only if the conditions are the same. What changed along the route going north?
Compare the temperature at which the Hyundai Inster stopped with the temperature range that the car that drove furthest went through. What does it tell about the conditions in which each drove?

criteria.text: Uses the source: the temperature fell along the route from $-7\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $-32\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, so the car that drove the furthest drove a large part of its distance on the coldest section and was in the frost the longest, whereas a car with a short range stopped already at the $-16\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ point.

criteria.detail: The cars did not drive in the same conditions, so the deviation is not only a property of the car and the cars cannot be ranked by their percentages.

parts.text: Assess why the range of a particular electric car in all winter conditions cannot be predicted from this one winter test. Name at least three factors that change the consumption. Tell also how the test should be changed to make the result more reliable.
hints: Which factors vary from one winter, route and driver to another and affect the consumption? What did this single test show about only one situation?

Look for factors in three groups: weather (for example temperature, wind), road and route, and car and driver. The data gives one example: compare the deviations of the two tests and their temperatures.
Think about how the test was carried out: how many times was each car driven, and were the conditions the same? How should the test be changed so that the spread of the results could be estimated?

criteria.detail: Names at least three factors that vary from one winter, route and driver to another and change the consumption: for example the temperature (in the test of 2025 the deviation was $18\,\%$, now $38\,\%$), wind, road surface, speed, the climbs of the route, preheating and the heating settings.

criteria.text: States that each car was driven only once, so the scatter of the results is not known, and proposes an improvement: the same, controlled conditions for all cars, several temperatures and repeats.

tasks.title: A skateboarder in a half-pipe
tasks.source_note: The situation and the numbers are invented examples.
tasks.text: A skateboarder of mass $45\,\text{kg}$ starts from rest at the rim of a half-pipe, at point A. They pass point B on the slope and arrive at the bottom, point C. The half-pipe has friction, and air resistance can be ignored. The zero level of potential energy is at point C. The bars in the figure show the skateboarder's potential energy and kinetic energy at points A, B and C. Along the track from A to C the distance is $3.4\,\text{m}$.

parts.text: How much internal energy has friction produced in the track and the skateboard's wheels from A to B and from A to C?
hints: Which forms of energy do the bars show? What should happen to their sum if there were no friction?

Mechanical energy is the sum of potential and kinetic energy: $E_\text{mech} = E_\text{p} + E_\text{k}$. Total energy is conserved, so the internal energy produced by friction is $\Delta E_\text{int} = E_\text{mech,A} - E_\text{mech}$.
At each of A, B and C read the height of both bars in joules and calculate the mechanical energy. Subtract it from the mechanical energy at A, separately for B and for C.

criteria.detail: Both bars are read at each point: A $700\,\text{J}$ and $0\,\text{J}$, B $300\,\text{J}$ and $300\,\text{J}$, C $0\,\text{J}$ and $500\,\text{J}$.
$E_\text{mech} = E_\text{p} + E_\text{k}$ and $\Delta E_\text{int} = E_\text{mech,A} - E_\text{mech}$, because the total energy is conserved.
$100\,\text{J}$ and $200\,\text{J}$; the internal energy grows as the skateboarder goes on.

parts.text: Determine the skateboarder's speed at point C.
hints: Which form of energy is related to speed, and how much of it is there at C?
Kinetic energy is $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Solve the speed from it: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_\text{k}}{m}}$.
Read the kinetic energy at C from the bar and substitute it with the mass $m = 45\,\text{kg}$. Remember that energy is in joules: $1\,\text{J} = 1\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_\text{k}}{m}}$
$v \approx 4.7\,\text{m/s} \approx 17\,\text{km/h}$, two significant figures.

parts.text: How large is the average force of friction on the skateboarder from A to C?
hints: Friction does work on the skater. The change in which energy equals the work done by friction?
The work of friction equals the increase in internal energy: $\Delta E_\text{int} = Fs$, from which $F = \dfrac{\Delta E_\text{int}}{s}$.
Use the increase in internal energy of part a for the whole way from A to C and the distance $s = 3.4\,\text{m}$. Compare the result with the skater's weight $mg$ and judge whether it is reasonable.

criteria.detail: The work done by friction equals the increase of internal energy: $\Delta E_\text{int} = Fs$, so $F = \dfrac{\Delta E_\text{int}}{s}$
$F = \dfrac{200\,\text{J}}{3.4\,\text{m}} \approx 59\,\text{N}$
The skateboarder's weight is $45\,\text{kg} \cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \approx 440\,\text{N}$, so friction is about $13\,\%$ of it, a sensible size for a board on wheels.

parts.text: What would the skateboarder's speed at C be if there were no friction? Why is the real speed smaller?
hints: What energy does the skater have at the start and at the end if nothing were lost?
Without friction the mechanical energy is conserved: $E_\text{k,C} = E_\text{p,A}$, and from this $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_\text{p,A}}{m}}$.
Read $E_\text{p,A}$ from the figure and calculate the speed. Compare it with the speed of part b and explain the difference with energy: where does the energy that is not kinetic energy go?

criteria.detail: Without friction the mechanical energy is conserved: $E_\text{k,C} = E_\text{p,A}$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_\text{p,A}}{m}}$

criteria.text: Explains that friction turns part of the original $700\,\text{J}$ of energy, about $29\,\%$ or $200\,\text{J}$, into internal energy of the track and the wheels, which is transferred to the surroundings as heat. Only $500\,\text{J}$ of kinetic energy remains, so the speed is smaller ($4.7\,\text{m/s} < 5.6\,\text{m/s}$). No energy is lost.

tasks.title: Two devices on an energy meter
tasks.source_note: The devices and the numbers are invented examples.
tasks.text: The graph shows the electrical energy $E$ measured by an energy meter for two electrical devices, A and B, as a function of time. Device A is an electric radiator whose electrical energy is all transformed into internal energy of the room. Device B is the motor of a goods lift, which raises a $150\,\text{kg}$ load to a height of $20\,\text{m}$ during the $80\,\text{s}$ of the graph. The price of electricity is $0.16\,\text{€/kWh}$.

parts.text: Determine the electrical power of devices A and B.
hints: What does the steepness of the line on the graph tell? Which quantity is the change of energy in time?
Power is the rate of change of energy: $P = \dfrac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}$, which is the slope of the $(t,\,E)$ graph.
On each line choose a point far from the origin and read its time and energy. Convert the energy from kilojoules if needed and divide it by the time.

criteria.detail: A point far from the origin is read on each line: A $(80\,\text{s};\ 120\,\text{kJ})$ and B $(80\,\text{s};\ 40\,\text{kJ})$.
$P = \dfrac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}$, for steady transformation the slope of the $(t,E)$ graph.
$P_\text{A} = \dfrac{120\,\text{kJ}}{80\,\text{s}} = 1.5\,\text{kW}$ and $P_\text{B} = \dfrac{40\,\text{kJ}}{80\,\text{s}} = 0.50\,\text{kW}$
$P_\text{A} = 1.5\,\text{kW}$ and $P_\text{B} = 0.50\,\text{kW}$; A's power is three times B's because its line is three times as steep.

parts.text: Each device is used for $3.0\,\text{h}$ a day for $30$ days. How much does the electricity of each device cost during that time?
hints: What is the energy of a device when the total running time is known? How is energy converted to euros when the price is given per kilowatt-hour?
$E = Pt$ and the cost is $C = E\,p$, where $p = 0.16\,\text{€/kWh}$. The energy must be given in kilowatt-hours.
First calculate the total running time in hours ($30$ days, $3.0\,\text{h}$ a day). Use the powers of part a in kilowatts, so that $\text{kW} \cdot \text{h} = \text{kWh}$.

criteria.detail: $E = Pt$ and the cost $C = E \cdot p$, where $p$ is the price of electricity; the energy in kilowatt-hours.

$E_\text{A} = 1.5\,\text{kW} \cdot 90\,\text{h} = 135\,\text{kWh}$ and $E_\text{B} = 0.50\,\text{kW} \cdot 90\,\text{h} = 45\,\text{kWh}$, since the total time of use is $30 \cdot 3.0\,\text{h} = 90\,\text{h}$
The ratio of the costs equals the ratio of the powers, $22\,\text{€} : 7.2\,\text{€} \approx 3$, because the time of use and the price are the same.

parts.text: Determine the efficiency of the lift motor B.
hints: Which energy is the useful one in the lift motor, and which is the energy it takes?
$\eta = \dfrac{E_\text{useful}}{E}$, where the useful energy is the change in the potential energy of the load, $E_\text{useful} = mgh$.
Calculate the useful energy and read the electrical energy taken by B in $80\,\text{s}$ from the graph. Use the same unit when you divide.

criteria.detail: $\eta = \dfrac{E_\text{useful}}{E}$, where the useful energy is the change in the load's potential energy $E_\text{useful} = mgh$.
The electrical energy taken by B in $80\,\text{s}$ is read from the graph: $E = 40\,\text{kJ}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_\text{useful} &= 150\,\text{kg} \cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \cdot 20\,\text{m} \\
&\approx 29.4\,\text{kJ} \\
\eta &= \dfrac{29.4\,\text{kJ}}{40\,\text{kJ}} \\
&= 0.74
\end{aligned}
$$
$\eta \approx 74\,\%$, two significant figures; the efficiency is below $100\,\%$.

parts.text: How large is the power transferred from motor B to the surroundings as heat? Into which form of energy does it first change?
hints: The motor takes energy, but only part of it goes to lifting the load. What else happens to the energy? In what form is it?
The loss power is the power taken minus the useful power: $P_\text{loss} = P - P_\text{useful}$, where $P_\text{useful} = \dfrac{E_\text{useful}}{t}$.

First calculate the useful power that goes into lifting the load in $80\,\text{s}$ and subtract it from the electric power $P_\text{B}$ of part a. Then think into which form of energy the loss first changes and how it gets to the surroundings.

criteria.detail: $P_\text{loss} = P - P_\text{useful}$, where $P_\text{useful} = \dfrac{E_\text{useful}}{t}$

criteria.text: States that the rest of the energy does not disappear but first becomes internal energy of the motor, gearbox and rope (friction and electrical resistance), which is transferred to the surroundings as heat.
